title: Glassware and cellaring
lead: The right glass for each beer, and the few beers that get better with age.

sections.name: How to cellar
sections.source: Craft Beer & Brewing, Brewing Dictionary (from The Oxford Companion to Beer)

keyPoints.line: keeps the hand from warming it.

read.bigIdea: The glass is part of the beer.
read.where: Cicerone’s rules: **stronger** beers go in **smaller** glasses, always leave room for a proper **head**, and the shape follows the style’s tradition. Shape changes the drink: a **bowl** collects aroma and lets you swirl, a thin **flared rim** delivers the beer cleanly, and a **stem** keeps the hand from warming it. In a pinch, a **white wine glass** works for most specialty beers.
read.mixup: A thick shaker pint is easy to stack, but it does nothing for aroma or head.
read.sayIt: It’s about 10%, so it comes in a smaller glass.

keyPoints.line: tall, room for the big head.

read.bigIdea: Know the glass for each style.
read.where: The **weizen** glass is tall with extra headspace for wheat beer’s big foam (usually half a liter). The **tulip**, a stemmed glass with a wide bowl and flared lip, suits rich, strong beers. A **goblet** or **chalice** is the Trappist glass. The **snifter** is for the strongest: barley wine, imperial stout. The **stange** (about 200 ml) is the Kölsch glass. The **nonic pint**, with its bulge, is the English pub glass for bitter, pale ale and stout. A **flute** suits lambic and gueuze.
read.mixup: A pilsner glass is tall and straight; a weizen glass curves out at the top for foam.

keyPoints.line: barley wine, imperial stout, old ale.

read.bigIdea: Most beer won’t improve. A few will.
read.where: A beer worth keeping should be **strong**, **sour** or **smoked**: alcohol, acid and smoke protect it. Good candidates: **barley wine**, **imperial stout**, old ale, strong **dark Belgian** ales, **lambic** and **gueuze**. Dark beers usually age better than pale. **Don’t** age **hop-forward** beers (Russian River prints “do not age” on Pliny the Elder) or fresh **wheat** beers: their best flavors fade.
read.mixup: “Vintage” on a beer list means the year it was brewed, and only for beers built to age.

keyPoints.line: standing before you pour an old bottle.

read.where: Keep aging beer at about **52–55°F**, in the **dark**, **upright**. Crown caps and Champagne-style corks don’t need the bottle on its side. Stand an old bottle **upright for 24 hours** before opening and pour carefully off the sediment. Over time, bready malt turns **nutty**, then **toffee** and **sherry**; hops **fade**. Signs it’s past its best: thin body, **cardboard**, or lost carbonation. **Bottle-conditioned** beers, with live yeast, age best.
read.mixup: Wine lies down; beer stands up.
read.sayIt: This is the 2023 bottle: rounder and more toffee than the new one.
